overview:
In 618 a Sui general named Li Yuan took the capital at Chang'an and declared a new dynasty, inheriting the reunified empire the Sui had built and squandered. His son, who seized the throne in 626 and ruled as Taizong, turned that inheritance into something larger: armies pushed deep into the Tarim Basin and the steppe, Turkic confederations acknowledged him as khagan as well as emperor, and a compact administrative machine — the Three Departments and Six Ministries, an equal-field system that assigned land to peasant households, a legal code copied later in Korea, Japan and Vietnam — extended the court's reach further than any Chinese state had managed in centuries. Recruitment through written examination widened, though in practice the great aristocratic clans of the northwest kept their grip on high office. The dynasty was interrupted once, from 690 to 705, by Wu Zetian, who ruled in her own name as emperor rather than as regent, the only woman ever to do so; almost everything written about her comes from later historians who found the fact intolerable, and her reputation has been argued over ever since.

Chang'an under Emperor Xuanzong, who came to the throne in 712, was probably the largest city on earth, a grid of walled wards holding Sogdian merchants, Japanese and Korean students, Persian refugees, Nestorian Christian and Zoroastrian and Manichaean congregations, and an enormous Buddhist establishment of monasteries and landholdings. Silk moved west along the overland routes and porcelain and tea south by sea; the sancai glazed tomb figures of camels and foreign grooms that fill museum cases today are the residue of that traffic. It was also the age of Li Bai, Du Fu and Wang Wei, and of woodblock printing, which the Tang used first for Buddhist texts. The high point ended abruptly. In 755 An Lushan, a frontier commander of Sogdian and Turkic descent who held three military governorships at once, marched on the capital; the emperor fled to Sichuan, and the war that followed dragged on to 763, ending only with Uyghur help. Tibetan forces sacked Chang'an in 763. The old land and tax systems never recovered, and the empire's later century and a half was a bargain between a court funded by salt monopolies and a north-eastern belt of hereditary military governors, the jiedushi, who taxed and soldiered on their own account. Emperor Wuzong's confiscation of Buddhist monastic wealth in the 840s, the enormous Huang Chao rebellion of the 870s and 880s, and the rise of the warlord Zhu Wen finished the arrangement; Zhu deposed the last Tang emperor in 907.

The scale of the damage is genuinely uncertain. Registered population fell from roughly nine million households before the An Lushan rebellion to under two million a few years after, and that collapse has been recycled as a death toll of thirty-six million or more. Most specialists treat the figures as a record of the state losing the ability to count and tax its subjects — through flight south, through governors who simply stopped reporting — rather than a straightforward body count, even though the war and the famine and disease that followed were plainly catastrophic.
significance: The Tang became the template that later East Asia measured itself against. Its legal code, ministries and examination ideal were adopted wholesale in Japan's Nara and Heian states, in Silla Korea and in Vietnam, and the model of an empire governed by examined civil officials rather than a hereditary warrior nobility outlived the dynasty by a thousand years in China itself. Its poetry became the permanent core of the Chinese literary canon. Its collapse mattered nearly as much as its success: the destruction of the old aristocratic families and the equal-field system cleared the ground for the very different Song order of commerce, printing and a genuinely competitive examination bureaucracy. And for roughly a century the Tang held one end of a continuous corridor of exchange running from the Yellow River to Abbasid Baghdad — a connectedness that the defeat at Talas in 751 and the wars after 755 pinched off, and that later Chinese writers would remember as a lost openness.
coverage: Written from general reference and institutional overviews rather than the Chinese primary record; the dataset holds no events at all for this story, so nothing here is anchored to a mapped place or date. The surviving record itself is heavily court-centred and retrospective — the standard histories were compiled by later dynasties with their own verdicts to deliver, which particularly distorts Wu Zetian and the rebel leaders — and post-755 population, tax and provincial data are fragmentary enough that basic questions about how many people died and how much territory the court actually controlled remain open.
